input_query: Which previous consultation paper does Policy Statement PS24/2 provide feedback on, and what is the paper's primary focus?
ground_truth_facts: Policy Statement PS24/2 provides feedback and final rules in response to Consultation Paper 23/13 (CP23/13).
The primary focus of Policy Statement PS24/2 is strengthening protections for borrowers in financial difficulty regarding consumer credit and mortgages.

input_query: What key proposals and customer groups were covered in the May 2023 consultation (CP23/13) regarding financial difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: CP23/13 consulted on rules to strengthen protections for mortgage, consumer credit and overdraft customers in financial difficulty.
The consultation proposed incorporating aspects of the coronavirus Tailored Support Guidance (TSG) into the Handbook, along with further targeted changes to support customers.

input_query: What were the FCA's findings in the November 2022 Borrowers in Financial Difficulty (BiFD) report?
ground_truth_facts: The November 2022 BiFD report outlined that while some firms were delivering good outcomes for borrowers in difficulty, many firms were falling short of expectations, resulting in harm.

input_query: How do the rules and guidance regarding payment difficulties advance the consumer protection objective?
ground_truth_facts: They aim to reduce and prevent harm to consumers who are in or at risk of payment difficulties by ensuring they receive appropriate support.
They require firms to consider the needs of different consumer groups, particularly vulnerable consumers who may be at greater risk of harm, and take appropriate action to mitigate these risks.

input_query: What targeted additional changes were proposed for mortgage firms regarding customers in payment shortfall?
ground_truth_facts: Changing guidance to allow firms more scope to capitalise payment shortfalls where appropriate.
Improving disclosure for all customers in payment shortfall.
Making clearer the existing requirement to record telephone calls with customers in payment shortfall, including video conferencing.

input_query: What specific amendments are being finalised for mortgage firms regarding statements under MCOB 13.5 and forbearance options?
ground_truth_facts: Under MCOB 13.5, firms will be required to send regular statements to all customers in arrears, regardless of whether the payment shortfall attracts charges.
Proposed guidance is changed so that mortgage firms should be transparent about the range of forbearance options they may consider, rather than will consider.

input_query: What specific approach is being taken regarding the proposed guidance on charges under CONC 7.7.6G for credit firms?
ground_truth_facts: The guidance proposed under CONC 7.7.6G (2) and (3) on charges is not being introduced.
The guidance originally proposed under CONC 7.7.6G(1) is being introduced with amendments relating to the frequency and nature of events to which the charges relate.

input_query: What number is specified in the excerpt of the regulation?
ground_truth_facts: The regulation text specifies the number 5.

input_query: How long is the implementation period granted to firms for the final rules, and why was this duration chosen?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are given just over 6 months to implement the changes.
The regulator considers this timeframe sufficient because many of the Handbook changes make permanent existing expectations under the TSG that have already become industry good practice.

input_query: How will the regulator use market and regulatory data and intelligence to assess firms regarding customers in financial difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: The regulator will use market and regulatory data and intelligence to identify outlier firms and products.
The regulator will use this data to assess the support and outcomes received by customers in financial difficulty.
The regulator will monitor complaints and information received from the Financial Ombudsman Service concerning the treatment of customers in financial difficulty.

input_query: When do the rules specified in the policy statement come into force, and what action will be taken regarding the TSG?
ground_truth_facts: The rules come into force on 4 November 2024.
The TSG will be withdrawn at the same time the rules come into force.

input_query: To which customers did the regulator propose extending the scope of the rules and guidance in CONC 7 and MCOB 13?
ground_truth_facts: The regulator proposed extending CONC 7 and MCOB 13 protections to customers who indicate that they are at risk of missing a payment.
The regulator proposed extending CONC 7 and MCOB 13 protections to customers where being at risk of missing a payment is otherwise identified by a firm.

input_query: What challenges and suggestions did stakeholders raise concerning the proactive identification of customers in emerging payment difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: Some consumer bodies favored a stronger shift requiring lenders to proactively seek to identify customers in emerging difficulty, with one suggesting extending rules to include when firms are aware a customer is at risk of missing repayments.
Some firms and a trade body expressed concerns about proactive identification, noting many firms have limited information to identify customers in the early stages of payment difficulty.

input_query: According to the feedback, what benefit would a more flexible approach to reporting to Credit Reference Agencies (CRAs) provide regarding customer engagement?
ground_truth_facts: A more flexible approach to reporting to CRAs was considered to help remove barriers to earlier engagement.

input_query: What is the finalised trigger point for firms to provide earlier support to customers approaching arrears under the rules and guidance?
ground_truth_facts: The scope of the rules and guidance is being expanded to cover customers approaching arrears.
The trigger point for earlier support is the point at which a customer indicates to the firm that they are at risk of not meeting one or more repayments when they fall due.

input_query: Do the proposed rules and guidance require firms to establish new systems or processes to proactively identify customers who may be in financial difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: The rules and guidance do not introduce new requirements on firms to take additional steps, or create new processes and systems, to identify customers who may be in financial difficulty.
The regulatory focus is on clarifying potential trigger points where firms should consider how to treat customers approaching arrears with forbearance and due consideration.

input_query: What action are customers encouraged to take if they experience a change in circumstances and consider their payments to be unaffordable?
ground_truth_facts: Customers are encouraged to contact firms if their circumstances change and they think their payments are becoming unaffordable.

input_query: What are lenders expected to do regarding credit reporting pending any changes following the Credit Information Market Study Final Report?
ground_truth_facts: Pending any changes following the report, lenders are expected to provide clear information on how they report information to customers' credit files.

input_query: According to feedback from consumer group representatives and debt advice bodies, why are struggling overdraft customers reluctant to self-identify?
ground_truth_facts: Struggling customers are reluctant to self-identify due to low awareness, anxiety, and stigma.
Struggling customers fear the potential negative impact of asking for help.

input_query: What is the official designation for the Government scheme known as 'Breathing Space' affecting customer overdraft facilities?
ground_truth_facts: 'Breathing Space' is the Government’s Debt Respite Scheme.

input_query: What actions and tools will the FCA deploy upon identifying serious misconduct in the consumer finance sector?
ground_truth_facts: Where the FCA identifies serious misconduct, it will use its most suitable tools to act, including supervisory intervention or enforcement.
The FCA will ensure that it takes the most appropriate and proportionate action as it progresses with its work.

input_query: According to existing rules CONC 6.7.2R and CONC 7.2.1R, what obligations do overdraft lenders already have regarding customers experiencing financial difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are required to monitor customers' accounts for signs of actual or possible repayment difficulties.
Firms must have appropriate policies and procedures in place for dealing with customers whose accounts fall into arrears.

input_query: Are firms required by regulatory rules to use specific, prescribed indicators to identify overdraft repeat use?
ground_truth_facts: Regulatory rules are not prescriptive about which specific indicators firms should use to identify repeat use.
Firms are responsible for developing their own repeat use strategies because they are best placed to understand their own overdraft lending book.

Firms are encouraged to use an appropriate range of indicators, including relevant information from personal current accounts (PCAs), to identify customers facing actual or potential financial difficulties.

input_query: What information from PCA activity can firms review alongside borrowing levels to better understand if a customer is facing or likely to face financial difficulties?
ground_truth_facts: Firms can consider information on changes in income levels.
Firms can consider information on changes in periodic payments.

input_query: What number is designated in the provided regulatory excerpt?
ground_truth_facts: The provided regulatory excerpt designates the number 11.

input_query: Do the rules prescribe specific indicators, triggers, or timing and content for communications with customers experiencing financial difficulties?
ground_truth_facts: The rules do not prescribe particular indicators or triggers to identify customers in actual or potential financial difficulties.
The rules are not prescriptive regarding the timing, content, or channels used for customer communications.
Under CONC 5D.3.3G(2), firms have discretion to tailor the language and tone of communications to the circumstances of the individual customer.

input_query: Why were rules in CONC 5D introduced to monitor overdrafts rather than relying on CONC 7 or CONC 6.7.2R?
ground_truth_facts: Overdraft facilities cannot be in arrears and do not have fixed repayment requirements.
CONC 5D rules were introduced to establish expectations for how firms monitor overdrafts and provide appropriate support to overdraft borrowers requiring it.

input_query: What number is specified in the provided regulation text?
ground_truth_facts: The regulation text specifies the number 12.

input_query: What potential risk did a firm identify regarding offering forbearance to customers too early?
ground_truth_facts: Offering forbearance too early could create the risk of customers making decisions that lead to poor outcomes.
A customer could agree to an arrangement resulting in them paying more interest over the longer term.

input_query: What concerns did industry respondents raise regarding the proposed changes to communications and the provision of information?
ground_truth_facts: Industry respondents interpreted the proposals as a departure from the TSG's discretionary approach to early, tailored support, especially concerning communications.
Respondents argued the rule changes created more mandatory information requirements and reduced firms' scope to tailor communications and support for customers who may be at risk.

Respondents warned that the changes would lead to disproportionate and intrusive contact—particularly for customers with very small payment shortfalls—causing unnecessary stress, anxiety, and customer disengagement.

input_query: What are firms required to consider and document regarding policies and procedures for customers facing payment shortfall or financial difficulty under MCOB 13?
ground_truth_facts: Firms must have documented policies and procedures in place setting out how they will deal fairly with any customer in payment shortfall under MCOB 13.3.1R (2).

When establishing policies and procedures to support customers in financial difficulty, firms should consider their responsibilities under the Consumer Duty and act to deliver good outcomes to retail customers.
A firm should only agree an arrangement with a customer under MCOB 13 if it considers that arrangement to be appropriate.

input_query: What do the changes to MCOB 13.3.1R require firms to do regarding customers at risk of payment shortfall?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are required to consider support for customers who indicate they are at risk of falling into payment shortfall, or where the firm otherwise becomes aware that the customer may be at risk.
The changes to MCOB 13.3.1R do not prevent firms from responding flexibly to customers.

input_query: Under CONC 8.2.2G, which Principles is a firm likely to breach if it recommends an unaffordable debt solution to a customer?
ground_truth_facts: Recommending a debt solution which a firm knows, believes, or ought to suspect is unaffordable for the customer is likely to contravene Principle 2, Principle 6, and Principle 9.
Recommending an unaffordable debt solution may also contravene other Principles under CONC 8.2.2G.

input_query: What specific exemptions from affordability requirements did the FCA introduce under PS23/8 to support the Government's Mortgage Charter, and which contracts are excluded?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are exempted from affordability assessments when varying a mortgage contract to temporarily reduce capital payments (including to zero and paying interest-only) for up to 6 months.
Firms are exempted from affordability assessments when reversing a mortgage term extension within 6 months of it taking effect.
These exemptions can be used once per contract by any mortgage lender, excluding second charge and bridging loan contracts.

input_query: Does a customer's request for a contractual variation automatically require a firm to determine if the customer is at risk of a payment shortfall, and when must further support be considered?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are not required to determine if a customer seeking a contractual variation has, or is at risk of falling into, a payment shortfall, and the request itself does not indicate such risk.

If a customer applying for a variation has a payment shortfall or indicates they are at risk of falling into one, the firm must consider whether further support is needed and ensure it is appropriate to the customer's circumstances.

The requirement to consider offering tailored support where a firm otherwise becomes aware of a payment shortfall risk (MCOB 13.3.1 R(1A)(c)) does not apply when a customer requests a contractual change.

input_query: Does the requirement apply strictly to information provided directly by the customer, and what other information sources are included?
ground_truth_facts: The requirement applies to information the firm becomes aware of from sources other than the customer.
Covered non-customer sources include third-party debt advisers, current account information, and credit reference agency (CRA) data held by the firm.

input_query: What rule changes did the regulator propose in CP23/13 regarding policies and procedures under CONC 7 and MCOB 13 for customers experiencing payment difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: The regulator proposed a new rule in both CONC 7 and MCOB 13 requiring firms to ensure the effectiveness of policies and procedures established for customers in or at risk of payment difficulty.
The proposed rule requires firms to review their ongoing compliance with these policies and procedures at appropriate intervals.

input_query: According to the consultation text, what are examples of circumstances when a review may be appropriate?
ground_truth_facts: A review may be appropriate when there are changes in the economic environment.
A review may be appropriate in response to internal reviews.

input_query: Why has the regulator decided against defining specific intervals or minimum timeframes for firms to review their policies and procedures?
ground_truth_facts: Setting minimum periods between reviews could lead to situations where firms only conduct reviews in line with that minimum period.
Not defining appropriate intervals or specific instances for review allows firms the flexibility to conduct reviews that respond to internal and external factors.
The regulator wants firms to adopt an outcomes-focused approach rather than a prescriptive one.

input_query: What preferences and concerns did trade bodies express regarding terminology for customers in vulnerable circumstances in response to the proposals for CONC and MCOB?
ground_truth_facts: Two trade bodies preferred retaining the distinction between 'vulnerable' and 'particularly vulnerable' to reflect that vulnerability can be transient and varies in nature and impact.

One trade body expressed concern regarding the regulatory consequences of failing to apply the same standards where a customer's vulnerability may or may not significantly affect their ability to deal with the firm.

input_query: How does the FCA position FG21/1 vulnerability guidance alongside the Consumer Duty, and what concerns did respondents raise regarding the use of guidance rather than rules in CONC 7.3 forbearance provisions?
ground_truth_facts: The FCA affirmed that FG21/1 remains the primary guidance for treating vulnerable customers fairly, setting expectations under the Consumer Duty for practical action across product design, customer service, staff capability, and communications.

Consumer organisations argued that forbearance proposals in CONC should be introduced as binding rules rather than guidance to ensure firms proactively offer all suitable viable options and record evidence if none are suitable.

Respondents raised concerns regarding revisions to CONC guidance, including the removal of reference to an 'unexpected shock' in CONC 7.3.5G(3) and the need for clarity on what constitutes a 'reasonable period of time to repay the debt' under CONC 7.3.5G(4).

input_query: How has the FCA updated CONC guidance concerning forbearance options and the ongoing monitoring of forbearance arrangements?
ground_truth_facts: The FCA updated guidance in CONC 5 and CONC 7 by incorporating non-exhaustive forbearance examples from the Tailored Support Guidance (TSG) and removing restrictive text in CONC 7.3.5G(3) to allow a broader range of reasons for accepting reduced, token, or zero payments.

The guidance clarifies that firms must take reasonable steps to conduct reviews at appropriate intervals to ensure forbearance remains suitable and does not merely defer or exacerbate customer difficulties.
During periodic reviews of forbearance, firms are encouraged to assess whether alternative solutions, including debt write-offs, are needed for the customer's circumstances.

input_query: Are mortgage lenders required under MCOB to provide specific forbearance options such as waiving interest or capital whenever a borrower experiences financial difficulty?
ground_truth_facts: The rules and options listed in MCOB do not create an automatic entitlement for customers to receive specific measures such as interest or capital waivers, nor are lenders bound to offer every type of support in all cases.

The measures listed in MCOB, including waiving interest or capital, represent options that must form part of a firm's consideration of what support is appropriate and reasonable based on the customer's specific circumstances.
While industry stakeholders noted that listed options are not prescriptive and may not always be viable, consumer groups highlighted that the forbearance list in MCOB 13.3.4AR is not exhaustive.

input_query: How do the regulatory proposals relating to MCOB 13.3.4C and MCOB 13.3.4CG address the forbearance options available to mortgage customers, and what discretion do firms retain when evaluating these options?
ground_truth_facts: Under proposals and guidance associated with MCOB 13.3.4C and MCOB 13.3.4CG, firms are expected to be transparent about the non-exhaustive range of forbearance options considered, which may include waiving interest and/or capital where a mortgage is unsustainable.

Firms must take into account all available options to support customers but retain the discretion to dismiss options that are unreasonable, will not resolve the position, or where other options are more appropriate.

The regulatory framework does not mandate the waiving of capital or interest and does not impede a firm's right to repossess a property provided that all reasonable attempts to resolve the customer's position have failed.

input_query: How do consumer credit feedback discussions regarding forbearance options relate to the FCA's finalised rules for mortgages under MCOB 13.3.4AR?
ground_truth_facts: In consumer credit feedback, consumer bodies recommended aligning proposals with mortgages and overdrafts by publicising lists of forbearance options on firm websites.
For mortgages, the FCA finalised rules to expand the list of forbearance options in MCOB 13.3.4AR as consulted on.
The objective of the MCOB 13.3.4AR rule is to ensure mortgage firms consider a range of support tailored to individual customer circumstances for those with payment difficulties.

input_query: What is the FCA's position regarding the publication of available forbearance options on firms' websites for consumer credit and overdraft customers, and how should firms approach communication with these customers?
ground_truth_facts: The FCA does not intend to require firms to publicise a list of available forbearance options on their websites under CONC 7, finding that generic website information is less valuable than tailored support and clear individual communications.

Firms are expected to support customer engagement through appropriate, accessible channels, having regard to FG21/1 guidance for vulnerable customers who may find certain channels stressful or need more time.

Feedback regarding the transparency of forbearance options for overdraft repeat users in or at risk of financial difficulty aligned with the broader consumer credit position against mandatory website listings.

input_query: How do the regulator's stance and stakeholder feedback on publishing forbearance options on firms' websites differ between overdrafts and mortgages?
ground_truth_facts: For overdrafts, the regulator maintained that firms should set out available forbearance options on their websites due to the limited nature of the product, but decided not to proceed with guidance requiring eligibility criteria and interest rates (CONC 5D.3.3G(7)) to prevent confusing complexity.

For mortgages, under proposed guidance MCOB 13.3.4CG(2)(c), consumer groups supported displaying forbearance options on websites in plain English, whereas industry respondents advocated for a high-level approach of 'potential' options to prevent customer preconceptions, difficult conversations, or manipulation of circumstances.

input_query: According to regulatory research, why do customers generally prioritise mortgage payments, and what consequences do they understand may result from missing a payment?
ground_truth_facts: Customers generally prioritise making mortgage payments because falling behind could ultimately result in the loss of their home.
Customers generally understand that missing mortgage payments provides no benefit and will adversely affect their credit file.
Customers recognize that missing a mortgage payment will negatively impact their access to other financial products.

input_query: What feedback and concerns were raised by respondents regarding the FCA's proposed rules on customer communication and signposting for money guidance and debt advice?
ground_truth_facts: Respondents requested clarification that explaining the benefits of debt advice and money guidance does not constitute regulated 'debt counselling' or 'debt adjusting', alongside concerns that smaller firms may struggle with staff training and channel availability.

Stakeholders had mixed views on referencing the Money and Pensions Service (MaPS) strategic toolkit for creditors, with a trade body seeking its removal over concerns about product breadth and updates, while a consumer body supported it for fostering referral partnerships.

input_query: Under the finalised guidance, in what circumstances should firms communicate the benefits of debt advice and money guidance to customers, and does this obligation require firms to provide debt counselling?
ground_truth_facts: Firms should communicate information on debt advice and money guidance where appropriate, such as when a customer indicates they are likely to be in financial difficulty, fails to meet payments, or during other customer engagements.
Firms may deliver these communications through standardised methods—such as standardised letters, call scripts, or digital communications—rather than individually tailored messages.
Firms are only expected to provide a high-level summary of the potential benefits and availability of debt advice, and are explicitly not expected to provide regulated debt counselling.

input_query: How do FCA regulatory provisions and consultation feedback across consumer credit (CONC) and mortgages (MCOB) address firms engaging with customers and signposting or referring them to debt advice?
ground_truth_facts: Under consumer credit provisions, CONC 7.3.7A(G)(3) allows firms to refer customers seeking debt advice to other firms in addition to not-for-profit debt advice providers, subject to consistency with regulatory obligations.

Under mortgage proposals relating to MCOB 13.3.2AR, industry respondents raised concerns that gathering customer information and engaging on money guidance could inadvertently pull unauthorised firms across the regulatory perimeter into regulated debt counselling or debt adjusting.

While the FCA plans a wider review of debt advice rules under CONC 8, mortgage respondents warned that proposed engagement and disclosure rules under MCOB 13 could place increased demand on the debt advice sector.

input_query: How did the regulator respond to feedback regarding the requirement in MCOB 13.3.2AR(-1)(b) to effectively communicate the benefits of money guidance and debt advice, particularly regarding alignment with the Consumer Duty and permissions?
ground_truth_facts: Despite feedback suggesting the removal of the word 'effectively' to align with overall customer understanding under the Consumer Duty, the regulator finalised the rule requiring firms to effectively communicate the potential benefits of accessing free and impartial money guidance and debt advice.

The regulator explained that effective communication under the rule aligns with the Consumer Duty consumer understanding outcome by equipping customers with timely, understandable information to make informed decisions.

Complying with the communication requirement in MCOB 13.3.2AR(-1) does not require permission for the regulated activity of debt counselling because it does not steer the customer toward a particular course of action.

input_query: What information did the FCA propose firms should provide to credit customers prior to granting forbearance, and what key feedback did respondents raise regarding credit file reporting and customer options?
ground_truth_facts: The FCA proposed that firms must provide timely, clear, and understandable information considering individual characteristics to help customers understand their financial position, balance impact, and credit file implications before receiving forbearance.
Firms and trade bodies highlighted that they can only advise on the factual information reported to credit reference agencies, not the subsequent interpretation by agencies or other lenders.
A consumer body noted that the proposed provisions omitted a reference from the Tailored Support Guidance (TSG) regarding communicating a customer's options.

input_query: How did the regulator respond in CONC rules to consultation feedback regarding the transposition of Tailored Support Guidance (TSG) on communicating customer options and explaining credit file impacts?
ground_truth_facts: Following feedback that the transposed proposal omitted TSG references to communicating a customer's options, the regulator incorporated wording requiring firms to communicate options into CONC 7.3.13AG(2) and CONC 5D.3.11G(2).

Recognising that lenders cannot predict how others will interpret credit files, the regulator revised CONC 7.3.13AG(2) and CONC 5D.3.11G(2) by replacing 'implications for the customer's credit file' with 'how it is/will be reported to the customer's credit file'.

input_query: How do the regulatory passages address customer communications regarding debt and forbearance options, and how should individual circumstances be factored into the support provided?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are encouraged to clearly inform customers that merely discussing support options does not impact their credit file, while ensuring they understand the potential credit file and financial impacts if forbearance arrangements are agreed.

Regulators declined to set fixed indicative timeframes for customers to review their outstanding debt information, noting that the appropriate timeframe depends on individual circumstances and the potential need to implement support swiftly.

Both passages emphasize adapting approaches to customers' specific situations, reflected in the regulator's focus on varied individual circumstances for debt resolution and respondent feedback proposing that overdraft rules explicitly reference 'individual circumstances'.

input_query: When addressing customers in financial difficulty, what expectations and feedback apply to firms regarding the removal of overdrafts, customer engagement, and allowing time to consider financial arrangements?
ground_truth_facts: A lender should not remove an overdraft facility if information indicates doing so would cause financial hardship, and merely notifying a customer of potential removal where hardship is indicated is unlikely to be appropriate and may cause undue anxiety.

While Section 98A of the Consumer Credit Act allows termination of regulated open-end agreements, lenders must prioritize appropriate support, comply with CONC 5D, and continue engagement with non-responsive customers, though guidance does not require firms to increase overdraft debt for essential living expenses.

Consumer groups emphasized that customers must be given time to evaluate proposed arrangements given their long-term financial implications, with at least one consumer group stating that less than 7 days could be unreasonable.

input_query: How has the regulator responded to industry feedback concerning mortgage customer disclosures and consideration periods, and what concerns were raised regarding disclosure methods?
ground_truth_facts: A trade body raised concerns that removing the ability to provide compliance information in annual statements could lead to burdensome system changes without preventing customer harm.

Addressing concerns that lenders cannot predict how third parties interpret credit records, the regulator amended its final rule requirement from disclosing the 'implications for the customer’s credit file' to explaining 'how it will be reported to the customer’s credit file'.

The regulator decided against mandating a specific time period for customers to consider agreements before entering them, pointing instead to existing MCOB 13.3.3AR reasonable time requirements and Consumer Duty duties.

input_query: How do the regulatory updates across MCOB and CONC adjust the scope and timing of support for customers who are vulnerable or experiencing financial difficulties?
ground_truth_facts: Under MCOB 13.3.4AR(2) and the Consumer Duty, firms must communicate the implications of an arrangement before it is agreed rather than solely in an annual statement up to 12 months later, taking into account vulnerable customers who may need extra time or third-party support.

MCOB chapters are being consequentially amended so that references to customers in payment shortfall or arrears reflect that MCOB 13 now applies to the treatment of customers in payment difficulties more broadly.

For consumer credit, consequential amendments include updating CONC 5 to reflect Vulnerable Customer Guidance and extending certain post-contract requirements in CONC 6.7 to customers approaching arrears.

input_query: What are the regulatory objectives behind the proposed credit forbearance enhancements, and to which categories of SME borrowers do these protections extend under CONC 7?
ground_truth_facts: The regulatory proposals aim to reduce and prevent harm to customers who are in or at risk of payment difficulties by ensuring they are provided with appropriate support, with compliance costs considered proportionate to the benefits.

CONC 7 protections apply to SME lending where the borrower is a 'relevant recipient of credit' under the Regulated Activities Order, which includes partnerships of 2 to 3 persons not all of whom are bodies corporate and unincorporated bodies of persons that do not consist wholly of bodies corporate.

While enhanced protections apply to eligible SMEs (including sole traders and small partnerships under schemes such as the Bounce Back Loan Scheme), firms may need to account for different factors when delivering forbearance to SME customers compared to individual consumers.

input_query: Under the FCA's guidance on escalating balances, what actions must a firm take regarding interest and charges when a customer maintains a sustainable repayment arrangement, and how does this requirement adapt to changing customer circumstances?
ground_truth_facts: Where a sustainable repayment arrangement is agreed as a forbearance measure and the customer complies with its terms, the firm must suspend, reduce, waive, or cancel interest or charges to ensure the debt balance does not increase during the arrangement.
The required reduction, suspension, waiver, or cancellation of interest and charges may fluctuate across the term of the arrangement as the customer's financial circumstances change.
If a customer becomes capable of paying larger amounts under the repayment plan, the firm is not required to waive as much interest, fees, or charges to prevent the balance from escalating.

input_query: What feedback and requests for clarification did respondents raise regarding the guidance allowing firms to adjust or reduce the waiver of interest and charges if a customer's financial circumstances improve?
ground_truth_facts: While most respondents found the guidance practical, consumer bodies warned that improved circumstances do not automatically mean a customer can pay more, and they raised concerns that the guidance could lead to arbitrary application of interest charges without greater clarity.

A consumer body recommended that firms be required to provide advance notice before altering waived interest and charges to give customers time to rearrange their finances or report unconsidered budgetary factors.
A firm specifically requested additional guidance defining what constitutes a 'larger amount' and how lenders should determine an appropriate approach to waiving less interest and charges.

input_query: How has the regulator amended its proposed rule on escalating balances for customers in repayment arrangements, and what rationale was provided for this change?
ground_truth_facts: The regulator finalised the rule on escalating balances with an amendment removing the word 'suspend' to provide additional clarity for firms and customers.

The term 'suspend' was removed because it implies interest and charges could be temporarily held off and later reimposed, which could cause confusion and compound financial difficulty rather than facilitating a stable financial footing.
Under the finalised approach, preventing escalating balances in sustainable repayment arrangements involves firms waiving or writing off interest in certain circumstances rather than suspending it.

input_query: How should firms approach adjusting payment amounts and interest or fee waivers when a customer's financial circumstances improve during a repayment arrangement?
ground_truth_facts: When a customer's circumstances change and allow them to pay larger amounts under a repayment arrangement, firms must not increase payment amounts unilaterally and should only do so following appropriate customer engagement.
If a customer pays larger amounts under an updated arrangement, the firm is not required to waive as much interest, fees, or charges to prevent the debt balance from escalating.
Effective customer engagement is identified as key to achieving good customer outcomes, particularly when reviewing forbearance measures to ensure they remain appropriate.

input_query: Following consultation feedback on fees and charges for customers in payment difficulties, how did the FCA amend its proposed guidance under CONC 7.7.6G and align enforcement with the Consumer Duty?
ground_truth_facts: Although the FCA originally consulted on introducing supporting guidance under CONC 7.7.6G to assist firms in determining necessary and reasonable costs to meet the Consumer Duty price and value outcome, it decided not to introduce proposed CONC 7.7.6G (2) and (3) due to concerns that differing interpretations of 'administration costs' would create confusion.

Rather than implementing CONC 7.7.6G (2) and (3), the FCA highlighted general Consumer Duty expectations that firms assess whether charges appear unjustifiably or unreasonably high, including accounting for cost decreases resulting from electronic communications.

The FCA proceeded with introducing guidance under CONC 7.7.6G(1) with amendments clarifying that firms assessing reasonable costs may consider the frequency and nature of events and whether they directly arise from the customer being in default or arrears difficulties.

input_query: What feedback did respondents provide regarding the proposed requirement for sustainable repayment arrangements and the guidance on priority debts and essential living expenses?
ground_truth_facts: Most respondents broadly agreed with requiring sustainable repayment arrangements, though some requested clarification on what constitutes sustainability, how it distinguishes from token payments, and the meaning of 'priority debt'.

Consumer bodies suggested broadening the guidance on priority debts and essential living expenses and advocated referencing the Standard Financial Statement (SFS), whereas one firm objected that the SFS is time-consuming and argued for flexibility based on conversations.

A consumer body warned against imposing arbitrary time cut-offs for repayment arrangements to clear arrears, recommending instead that lengthy repayment terms be reviewed regularly as cost-of-living pressures ease.

input_query: What feedback and concerns did respondents raise regarding lengthy repayment terms and third-party debt solutions such as DMPs and IVAs in this section of the consultation feedback?
ground_truth_facts: Respondents noted that lengthy repayment terms can be reviewed regularly and payments potentially increased once cost-of-living pressures have eased in the future.

A respondent raised concerns that clients receiving debt advice could be committed to unaffordable third-party debt solutions, specifically referencing Debt Management Plans (DMPs) and Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs).
A respondent requested that the proposals clarify a creditor's responsibility regarding repayment proposals submitted as part of a DMP or IVA.

input_query: Under CONC guidance and rules on forbearance, how does the FCA classify token payments relative to sustainable repayment arrangements, and when might a sustainability assessment be omitted?
ground_truth_facts: Token payments are recognised as a forbearance option, but they are unlikely to qualify as a sustainable repayment arrangement because they typically do not enable the customer to repay the debt over a reasonable period of time.

Firms must take all reasonable steps to ensure agreed repayment arrangements are sustainable, taking into account priority debts and living expenses (including mortgage, rent, council tax, food, and utility bills).
A formal sustainability assessment may not be needed where a customer's circumstances mean they can only make small token payments to acknowledge the existence of the debt.

input_query: How did the FCA modify and clarify its proposed guidance on reviewing forbearance measures in response to consultation feedback about review frequency?
ground_truth_facts: In response to feedback that frequent reviews create emotional strain and operational burden, the FCA amended its supporting guidance in CONC 7 and CONC 5D to state that reasonable steps 'may include' reviews at appropriate intervals, replacing the proposed 'likely to include'.

The FCA finalised the rule requiring firms to take reasonable steps to ensure forbearance remains appropriate, but clarified that no further in-depth review may be needed if a customer is meeting the terms of the arrangement and has not indicated any difficulty.

The FCA expects firms to engage customers and consider further reviews of forbearance appropriateness if customers report changed circumstances or if monitoring reveals they are struggling to meet the arrangement.

input_query: What industry concerns and alternative proposals were raised regarding the requirement for firms to provide customers with a record of their completed income and expenditure assessments?
ground_truth_facts: Four trade bodies, several firms, and one consumer organisation disagreed with the proposed guidance requiring firms to make a record of income and expenditure assessments available to customers.
Concerns were raised that certain firms lack the system capabilities to share records and that imposing a mandatory requirement would introduce unnecessary costs and complexity.

Trade bodies suggested adopting the existing Tailored Support Guidance (TSG) wording into CONC, which qualifies that firms should share or make available records 'where possible and within its existing systems capabilities'.

input_query: What are the regulator's finalized rules and guidance regarding how firms conduct income and expenditure assessments and share or re-use those assessment records?
ground_truth_facts: Firms are not mandated to perform income and expenditure assessments, but any assessments undertaken must be carried out objectively and may have regard to the Standard Financial Statement (SFS) or an equivalent tool.

Firms are not required to build new systems to share records, but under CONC 7.3.7AG(4), they should make assessment records available to customers where possible to facilitate sharing with other lenders and debt advice providers.

While firms do not have to rely on information gathered by third parties, they should support and encourage customers to re-use up-to-date assessment information where appropriate, such as using an assessment completed by another lender.
